intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · food to nerves
Grade 10 is the human-systems year. Grade 11 then does endocrine, reproduction, skeleton, muscle, homeostasis and plants. Write every organ as *structure → function → what goes in / what comes out*.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Carbohydrates
body: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The elements are in the of 1 C: 2 H:1 O.
Carbohydrates are obtained from sugar cane, milk, bread, potatoes, wheat, pasta, cereals, “injera” and rice.
Monosaccharides join together to form complex carbohydrate molecules, such as disaccharides and polysaccharides, through the process of condensation.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Proteins
body: Just as monosaccharides are the building blocks of polysaccharides, amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
All amino acids contain an amino group (-NH2), which consists of hydrogen and nitrogen.
Proteins are referred to as nitrogenous compounds, because of the presence of nitrogen in their structure.
The bond between two amino acids is called a peptide bond.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Lipids
body: The most common lipids are fats, oils and waxes.
Like carbohydrates, lipids are composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Fats and oils are similar except that fats are solid, while oils are liquid at room temperature.
Fats produce more energy than carbohydrates or proteins.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Minerals
body: Minerals (mineral salts) are important inorganic compounds containing elements which are essential for normal body metabolism.
Examples of mineral elements are iron, calcium, potassium, etc.
Animals obtain these elements from the foods they take in.
Place a small amount of bean seed in a metal cup (crucible). b.

cards.title: 1.1.5 Vitamins
body: Vitamins are organic substances that are important for normal growth and development.
Vitamins are required in very small amounts (traces) in the diet, but their role is vital.
Vitamins were named A, B, C, D, E and K, in order of their discovery, but they are also given chemical names.
Vitamins do not supply energy nor do they help in building the body.

cards.title: 1.1.6 Water
body: Water is the most important nutrient of all living cells.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.
Life on the earth is totally dependent on water.
Water is essential to the existence of living organisms anywhere.

cards.title: Worked example: daily energy needs
cards.problem: An 18-year-old male needs about 14 200 kJ of energy per day. One day he eats breakfast (2 500 kJ), lunch (4 800 kJ) and dinner (4 200 kJ). Has he met his energy requirement? If not, how much more does he need?

steps.text: Step 1: add the energy eaten: 2 500 + 4 800 + 4 200 = 11 500 kJ.
Step 2: compare with the requirement: 14 200 − 11 500 = 2 700 kJ.
Step 3: he is 2 700 kJ short. If this continued, his body would use stored fat (and later protein) for energy and he would lose mass.
Note: an 18-year-old female needs about 9 600 kJ per day; energy needs depend on age, sex, body size and activity.

cards.answer: No — he needs about 2 700 kJ more.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following describes the chemical process of condensation when two glucose molecules are linked?

steps.text: Condensation is the formation of a larger molecule by releasing a water molecule.
For example, two glucose molecules can be condensed and linked to form one molecule of disaccharide.

cards.answer: The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following organic compounds is defined as 'nitrogenous' due to the consistent presence of nitrogen in its chemical structure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review chemical elements of each compound**
* Carbohydrates (monosaccharides and polysaccharides) contain only Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen ($$\text{C, H, O}$$).
* Lipids contain only Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen ($$\text{C, H, O}$$).
* Proteins contain Carbon, Hydrogen, Oxygen, and Nitrogen ($$\text{C, H, O, N}$$).

**Step 2: Recall the key facts**
Proteins are referred to as nitrogenous compounds, because of the presence of nitrogen in their structure."

**Final Result:**
**Proteins**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary role of the hydrochloric acid (HCl) produced by the gastric glands in the stomach wall?

options.A: To chemically emulsify large fat droplets into tiny lipids.
options.B: To provide an acidic medium (pH 1.5) that activates pepsinogen and kills bacteria.
options.C: To lubricate the lining of the esophagus for peristalsis.
options.D: To neutralize the alkaline bicarbonate ions entering from the pancreas.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze stomach gastric secretions**
the stomach wall secretes gastric juice containing mucus, hydrochloric acid ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH 1.5), and pepsinogen.

**Step 2: Identify the function of HCl**
* It provides an acidic medium (pH of about 1.5) required for the active protease enzyme pepsin to work.
* It activates the precursor **pepsinogen** into the active enzyme **pepsin**.
* It kills bacteria present in the food and dissolves minerals.

**Final Result:**
**To provide an acidic medium (pH 1.5) that activates pepsinogen and kills bacteria.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All biological molecules are organic and should must have
cards.why:
**Logic:**
By definition, **organic molecules** are compounds that contain **carbon** atoms bonded to **hydrogen** atoms (hydrocarbons). While they often contain oxygen, nitrogen, or phosphorus, C and H are the core requirements for a molecule to be considered organic.

**Result:**
Carbon and Hydrogen.

cards.title: Using the energy table
body: Energy from a food = mass of each nutrient (g) × its energy value (kJ/g), added together. Example: 10 g fat gives 10 × 38.0 = 380 kJ, more than twice the energy of 10 g of carbohydrate (171 kJ).

cards.title: Nutrients — what each one is for
body: **Digestion** breaks large insoluble food into small soluble pieces that can cross membranes. Mechanical = teeth, churning, bile emulsifying fat. Chemical = enzymes (each enzyme is picky about substrate and pH).

cards.title: The tube
body: Mouth (amylase on starch) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (acid + pepsin on protein) → small intestine (bile from liver/gall bladder; pancreatic amylase, trypsin, lipase; wall enzymes finish the job; villi absorb) → large intestine (water back into blood) → egestion of faeces.

cards.title: Liver and pancreas are side-offices that dump chemicals into the small intestine. They are not “the tube” itself.
Enzymes by address
body: Mouth = starch. Stomach = protein (needs acid). Small intestine = all three (carb, protein, fat) + bile for fat droplets. “Small intestine does the real absorbing — villi.”

cards.title: More detail — nutrients and the tube
body: Carbohydrates: sugars are already small; starch is a chain that amylase chips into maltose, then maltase finishes glucose. Proteins: pepsin (stomach, pH ~2) and trypsin (intestine, alkaline) cut to peptides, peptidases to amino acids. Fats: bile salts from the liver emulsify (big drops → tiny drops, more surface); lipase then cuts to fatty acids and glycerol. Bile is not an enzyme.

Liver: makes bile, stores glycogen, processes incoming blood from the gut (hepatic portal vein). Pancreas: digestive juice + (later) insulin. Appendix is a dead-end off the caecum — know it exists; don’t invent a major job.

Deficiency sketches: no vitamin C → scurvy; no D / Ca → weak bone; no iron → anaemia; no iodine → goitre (ties to Grade 11 thyroid); no protein in children → wasting. Excess sugar/fat → obesity and later diabetes risk.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Ingestion, Digestion and Egestion
body: The term “soluble” means that a substance can dissolve in a liquid.
Ingestion is the act of eating or taking in food through the mouth.
The break down of large food particles into small, usable molecules is called digestion.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Mechanical and Chemical Phases of Digestion
body: Most often, the food an animal consumes is in large pieces.
The mechanical phase is only a physical change, because the chemical composition of the food remains the same.
Teeth help in the physical (mechanical) breakdown of food, by biting, crushing and grinding.

cards.title: 1.2.4 The Pharynx
body: The pharynx (throat) is a muscular tube connecting the mouth to the oesophagus (gullet), and the nasal cavity to the trachea (windpipe).
The pharynx is located at the back of the mouth, and transports food to the oesophagus.
The tongue rolls food into small round masses called boluses (singular: bolus).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An 18-year-old male needs about 14 200 kJ per day, but an 18-year-old female needs about 9 600 kJ. What is the main reason for the difference?

options.A: Males usually have a larger body mass with more muscle, so a higher metabolic rate
options.D: Females digest food twice as efficiently

cards.why: Energy needs depend on body size, muscle mass, growth and activity. On average males have a larger body and more muscle tissue, which respires more, so they need more energy each day. Both sexes respire and store fat.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the chemical process of condensation when two glucose molecules are linked?

options.A: The breakdown of a large carbohydrate molecule into two monosaccharides by adding a water molecule.
options.B: The physical chewing and grinding of starch in the oral cavity to increase surface area.
options.C: The reaction of glucose with Benedict's solution at high temperatures to form copper oxide.
options.D: The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define condensation**
condensation is the formation of a larger molecule by releasing a water molecule. For example, two glucose molecules can be condensed and linked to form one molecule of disaccharide.

**Step 2: Use the chemical equation**
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Condensation}} C_{12}H_{22}O_11 + H_2O$$
This clearly shows two monosaccharides linking to form a larger disaccharide and a water molecule.

**Final Result:**
**The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.**

cards.q: In humans, most of the food digestion process takes place in the
cards.why: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine where most chemical digestion occurs as it receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juice.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: Physical change of large droplets of fats in to smaller droplets by bile is:  A) Digestion  B) Peristalsis  C) Emulsification  D) Elimination  E) None

steps.text: **Step 1.** **Emulsification** is the process where bile salts break down large fat globules into smaller droplets.
**Step 2.** This is a **physical change** that increases the surface area for lipase enzymes to act upon.

tips.text: Most animals, particularly humans, need a balanced diet, which should include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, minerals, vitamins and water.
A balanced diet, obtained from food sources, provides energy, and materials for growth and normal body functioning.

Water should not be thought of as a simple nutrient because it has a wide variety of functions in the body of an organism. It acts as a solvent, is essential in cooling the body, provides a medium of transport and facilitates hydrolysis in all living organisms.
The amount of energy required by a person depends on age, gender, body size and the type of work the person does.
Humans need different minerals and vitamins in their diet for normal body metabolism and food health (well-being).
If we lack one or more mineral nutrients or vitamins in our diet, we can easily suffer from serious deficiency diseases.

questions.answer: Fuel. Broken to glucose; burnt in respiration for ATP.
why: Carbohydrates (starch, sugars) are digested to glucose, which cells oxidise in respiration to release energy as ATP — they are the body's main fuel.

similar.q: A dehydration reaction typically produces  A) nucleotide.  B) fatty acid.  C) protein.  D) amino acid.  E) glucose.
similar.a: C. protein. — Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in dehydration reactions to form polypeptides/proteins – a typical dehydration product. Fatty acids, amino acids and glucose are monomers, the products of HYDROLYSIS of lipids, proteins and starch. Answer: C.

questions.q: Why bile is not an enzyme.
questions.answer: It emulsifies fat (physical droplets). No chemical cut. Lipase does the chemical cut.

questions.q: Which nutrient family supplies $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ of energy and has building blocks that combine one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids?
questions.answer: C
why: **Identify the energy value.** The energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit) gives the energy yields per gram as carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and water $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$. Since lipids provide exactly double the energy of carbohydrates, the value $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ is the lipid value.

**Identify the building blocks.** The unit states that lipids are made of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acids through condensation reactions, which matches the second clue in the question.

questions.q: A student in Asmara eats a lunch of injera with shiro and boiled eggs containing $$80\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$25\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$12\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (b) State which nutrient supplies the greatest amount of energy and give that amount.
questions.answer: (a) The meal releases $$2374\text{ kJ}$$ of energy in total. (b) Carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, $$1368\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** The energy released by a nutrient equals its mass in grams multiplied by its energy yield per gram from the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit), so total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$).
**Calculate the energy from carbohydrates.** Energy from carbohydrates = $$80\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1368\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the energy from proteins.** Energy from proteins = $$25\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 550\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the energy from lipids.** Energy from lipids = $$12\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 456\text{ kJ}$$.
**Add the three values.** Total energy = $$1368\text{ kJ} + 550\text{ kJ} + 456\text{ kJ} = 2374\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the contributions.** The contributions are carbohydrates $$1368\text{ kJ}$$, proteins $$550\text{ kJ}$$ and lipids $$456\text{ kJ}$$. Since $$1368 > 550 > 456$$, carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, even though lipids have the highest energy value per gram, because far more carbohydrate was eaten.

questions.q: A person eats a meal of fried fish. Describe the complete journey of the fish proteins from the mouth until their digestion products reach the liver. In your answer name each enzyme that acts on the proteins, the pH condition in each region, and the blood vessel that carries the products to the liver.
questions.answer: In the mouth the fish is only chewed and made into a bolus because saliva contains amylase, not a protein enzyme. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which breaks the proteins into polypeptides. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) the pancreatic enzyme trypsin breaks them into peptides, and in the ileum peptidase releases amino acids. The amino acids are absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries and are carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
why: **Mouth and esophagus: mechanical preparation only.** The teeth chew the fish (mastication) and the tongue rolls it into a bolus, which is pushed into the pharynx and moves down the esophagus by peristalsis. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch and not on protein, so no chemical digestion of protein occurs here.

**Stomach: acid activation of pepsin.** Food enters the stomach through the cardiac sphincter. The gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 (about 1.5 to 2.0), mucus and pepsinogen. The acid kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which hydrolyses the fish proteins into polypeptides, while mucus protects the stomach wall from being corroded or digested.

**Duodenum: alkaline conditions and trypsin.** The partially digested food passes into the duodenum, where bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) neutralizes the acidic chyme and creates an alkaline environment of about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice adds trypsin, which continues the hydrolysis of proteins into shorter peptides.

**Ileum: peptidase and absorption through villi.** Intestinal juice in the ileum contains peptidase, which hydrolyses the peptides into amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed through the single layer of epithelial cells covering the villi into the network of blood capillaries inside each villus; the central lacteal of the villus absorbs fats instead, not amino acids.

**Hepatic portal vein: delivery to the liver.** The capillaries of the villi join to form the hepatic portal vein, which carries the amino acids directly to the liver. The liver acts as a central checkpoint that sorts amino acids, regulates glucose levels and detoxifies harmful chemicals before the blood is distributed to the rest of the body.

questions.q: Describe how the starch in a plate of injera is digested and absorbed from the mouth until the glucose reaches the liver, naming each enzyme involved and stating the pH conditions under which it works.
questions.answer: In the mouth, salivary amylase (ptyalin) at neutral pH (about 7.0) digests starch into maltose. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 denatures salivary amylase so starch digestion stops. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) pancreatic amylase digests starch into maltose, and in the ileum maltase digests maltose into glucose, which is absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries of the hepatic portal vein and carried to the liver.
why: **Mouth: salivary amylase at neutral pH.** Chewing with the teeth increases the surface area of the injera, and saliva supplies salivary amylase (ptyalin), which hydrolyses starch into maltose at a neutral pH of about 7.0. The tongue forms a bolus that is swallowed and moved down the esophagus by peristalsis.

**Stomach: the enzyme is denatured.** In the stomach the bolus mixes with gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 to 2.0. This extreme acidity denatures salivary amylase, so starch digestion stops completely, and gastric juice contains no enzyme that acts on starch.

**Duodenum: pancreatic amylase in alkaline conditions.** Bile from the liver neutralizes the acidic chyme and makes the duodenum alkaline, about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice supplies pancreatic amylase, which resumes the hydrolysis of starch into maltose at this optimum alkaline pH.

**Ileum: maltase releases glucose.** Intestinal juice in the ileum contains maltase, which hydrolyses maltose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed through the epithelium of the villi into the blood capillaries inside them.

**Transport to the liver.** The capillaries of the villi drain into the hepatic portal vein, which carries the absorbed glucose directly to the liver, where the glucose level of the blood is regulated before the blood passes to the rest of the body.

questions.q: Explain how the lipids in a spoonful of butter are digested and absorbed, and name the vessel inside the villus that carries their digestion products away.
questions.answer: No chemical digestion of the butter occurs in the mouth or stomach, only mechanical churning. In the duodenum, bile salts emulsify the large fat droplets into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area, and the alkaline bile also provides the optimum pH for pancreatic lipase, which hydrolyses the fats into fatty acids and glycerol. These products are absorbed into the central lacteal of the villus and are carried away in the lymphatic system.
why: **Mouth and stomach: mechanical treatment only.** Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch, and gastric juice contains pepsin, which acts on proteins, so neither secretion can chemically digest the butter. The fat is only broken into smaller pieces mechanically by chewing and by churning in the stomach.

**Duodenum: emulsification by bile.** Bile from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains no enzymes but contains bile salts. These perform emulsification, physically breaking the large fat droplets into millions of tiny droplets, which greatly increases the surface area available to the enzyme.
**Optimum pH for lipase.** Bile is alkaline, so it neutralizes the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach and creates the alkaline conditions of about pH 8.0 in which pancreatic lipase works best.

**Chemical digestion by pancreatic lipase.** Pancreatic juice supplies lipase, which hydrolyses the emulsified fat into fatty acids and glycerol. This is why bile is essential even though it contains no enzymes: without emulsification the lipase would have far too little surface area on which to act.

**Absorption into the lacteal.** The fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the central lymphatic capillary of the villus called the lacteal, which carries them into the lymphatic system. This differs from the water-soluble products glucose and amino acids, which enter the blood capillaries of the villus and then the hepatic portal vein.
